pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of how the company's work flows through this workspace. Share it with the estimator, the production manager and each foreman.
What lives where
Customers
: homeowners, landlords, HOAs and insurance customers, with roof age, insurance carrier, what they owe, and open jobs.
Roof jobs
: inspections, repairs, replacements and storm work, with squares, pitch, roof system, foreman and crew, claim number, price and margin.
Materials
: shingles, underlayment, flashing, vents, fasteners and safety gear, and what needs ordering.
Invoices
: deposits, insurance first checks, depreciation and final bills.
A job from first call to paid
The call comes in; add the customer and a Roof job as
New request
, work type Roof inspection.
The estimator inspects, measures and prices it. A signed estimate becomes a replacement or repair job,
Scheduled
with a crew. A foreman can press
Assign to me
Send the deposit invoice when it is signed.
On the day, the crew works the production checklist.
Mark done
stamps the completion date. Send the final invoice that day.
Past-due invoices go to
Overdue
; the customer's Awaiting payment counts sent and overdue.
Mark paid
stamps the payment date.
Your rhythm
Every morning: Dashboard, today's crews, overdue invoices
Every afternoon: tomorrow's material drops and dumpsters
Every Friday: count materials and safety gear
Every month: callbacks and thin margins
Making it yours

Change roof systems, crews and work types to match your company, and delete the sample customers once a dozen of your own are in. Type in any cell or drag cards between columns; every total updates by itself.
Change orders and allowances

Replacement estimates carry allowances, such as a number of decking sheets. When the crew finds more, the foreman photographs it and the office tells the homeowner before the work is done. The extra goes on the final invoice with the photos, which is why a final bill can be higher than the original quote. Keep the quote on the job as signed, so the margin compares what you sold with what it cost.
Jobs by stage, revenue by type of job and unpaid invoices.
Overdue roof jobs
My roof jobs
Overdue invoices
Awaiting payment (sent and overdue)
Crew schedule, next 7 days
Leak callbacks
Roofs are sold on the roof, not on the phone. A careful inspection and a clear estimate win the job and protect your margin.
Booking the inspection
Add the lead as a customer. Ask the age of the roof, any leaks inside, and whether there was a recent storm. If yes, ask whether they have already called their insurer.
Book it as a Roof job with work type
Roof inspection
and give it to the estimator.
Ask for gate codes, dogs, and whether someone will be home to see the attic.
On the roof
Photos of every slope, ridge, valley, penetration and gutter run, plus a wide shot of the house
Count layers at an edge; two layers means a full tear-off
Walk the decking for soft spots and note where
Check flashing at chimneys, walls, skylights and pipe boots
Look at ventilation: intake at the soffits, exhaust at the ridge
In the attic: daylight, stains, wet insulation, mold, bathroom fans venting into the attic
Storm work: test squares on each slope, marked hits on soft metals and vents
Measuring
Measure each plane, add them, and enter the total in
Squares
(one square is 100 square feet). Add waste: about 10 percent on a simple gable, 15 percent or more on a cut-up hip roof. Set
Pitch
: steep roofs need more labor, safety gear and time, and you price them that way.
Building the estimate
Materials by the square for the chosen
Roof system
, plus underlayment, ice and water shield in valleys and eaves, drip edge, starter, ridge cap and vents.
Tear-off and disposal by the square and by the layer.
Decking replacement priced per sheet, with an allowance written on the estimate.
Labor by the square, adjusted for pitch and stories.
Permit, if your city requires one.
Enter the quote, material cost, labor cost and hours. The
Margin
column should land between 30 and 40 percent on a replacement; under 20 shows as Thin.
Presenting it

Show the homeowner the photos first, then the options: repair, replace with standard shingles, replace with a better system. Leave a written estimate with what is and is not included and a deposit amount. For insurance jobs, write the
Claim number
on the job and do not quote a price before the adjuster has scoped the loss.
Example

After a hailstorm, the estimator inspects a 1999 roof on a two-story home: 31 squares, walkable pitch, hits on every slope and the box vents. She photographs test squares, the homeowner files the claim, and the job waits for the adjuster meeting. The adjuster approves a full replacement, and the job moves to Scheduled with Crew B.
A replacement is a one or two day operation with a lot of moving parts. The crew that starts with a plan finishes on time, leaves a clean yard, and does not get a callback.
The day before
The production manager confirms the material drop: shingles, underlayment, flashing and vents on the driveway or the roof, not the lawn.
Book the dumpster and confirm where it goes.
Call the homeowner: start time, noise, cars out of the driveway, pets inside, valuables off the attic shelves and walls.
Check the forecast. Do not tear off more than the crew can dry in that day.
Morning checklist
Harnesses, anchors and ladders inspected; roof anchors set before anyone works an edge
Tarps over landscaping, plywood against windows and AC units
Magnetic sweeper on the truck
Foreman walks the roof with the crew and points out soft decking and problem flashing
During tear-off and install
Tear off one slope at a time; dry it in with underlayment before moving on.
Replace soft decking and write down how many sheets: it goes on the final invoice.
Ice and water shield in valleys and at the eaves, drip edge on eaves before underlayment and on rakes after.
New flashing at walls and chimneys; never reuse old step flashing.
Nail pattern by the manufacturer's sheet, especially in high-wind areas.
Before the crew leaves
Every penetration flashed and sealed, every vent installed
Gutters cleaned of granules and nails
Yard, driveway and beds swept with the magnet twice
Photos of the finished roof from every side
Foreman walks the job with the homeowner
Closing it out
Enter real material cost and hours on the job and press
Mark done
. Send the final invoice the same day. If the homeowner calls about a leak later, open a new job, tick
Leak callback
, and send the foreman who did the work. Review callbacks monthly: most come from flashing and pipe boots.
Example

Crew A tears off a 24-square duplex roof. At noon the foreman finds six soft sheets over the back porch, photographs them and calls the office, which tells the owner before they are replaced. The roof is dried in by four, shingled by noon the next day, and the yard is swept twice. Six sheets are added to the final bill exactly as the estimate's allowance said.
After a hailstorm or windstorm the phones ring for weeks. The companies that do well keep the same standards on the hundredth call as on the first, and keep claims organized.
The first 48 hours
Make a list of every customer in the storm path from Customers, starting with roofs older than 15 years.
Emergency calls first: active leaks and tree strikes. Tarp them the same day and mark the job
Emergency
Book free inspections in order. Do not promise a date you cannot keep.
Working with insurance
The homeowner files the claim; you never sign for them or promise a payout.
Write the
Claim number
on the job and the carrier on the customer.
Be on the roof for the adjuster meeting with your photos and test squares.
If the approved scope misses items (drip edge, code upgrades, damaged vents), send a supplement with photos, and put the job
On hold
until it is answered.
Insurance jobs usually pay in two parts: the first check before work, the depreciation after the final invoice and photos. Bill them as two invoices.
Tarping checklist
Photos before the tarp goes on
Tarp wide enough to go over the ridge
Battens screwed, not nailed through the tarp
Interior: buckets, and furniture moved away from drips
Customer told the tarp is temporary and how long it will hold
Keeping control of the schedule

Use the job calendar and the crew field. Two replacement crews can do roughly eight to ten average roofs a week in good weather; book to that number, not to the number of calls. Put the next available date in writing for every customer.
Watch out for
Out-of-town crews knocking doors in your area. Your advantage is being local and still here next year: say so.
Overloading the repair crew with inspections; give the estimator the inspections and keep the crew on tarps and repairs.
Cash flow: you buy materials before insurance pays. Keep an eye on Awaiting payment on the Dashboard.
Example

A June hailstorm hits the north side of town. The office finds 40 customers in the path and calls the oldest roofs first. Over the next two weeks the estimator inspects 30 roofs, 18 claims are opened, and each job carries its claim number. Three supplements are sent; two are paid within a month.
